title: Screen Solver mock quiz
description: Six problems covering the three ways a question can reach this app: on the screen, out of the speakers, or both at once. Read by test/fixtures/mock-quiz/quiz.ts (automated) and quiz-page.js (manual) -- one source of truth, no second copy to drift.

problems.why: The plain happy path: everything the answer needs is on the screenshot, and nothing is said out loud.

screen.title: Sum of Positive
statement: You get an array of numbers, return the sum of all of the positives ones.
Note: if there is nothing to sum, the sum is default to 0.

expected.title: Sum of Positive
expected.notes: The signature must be the one in the editor pane -- positiveSum(arr), not sumPositive or numbers. The empty-array case is called out in the notes and the sample tests, so it has to be handled rather than assumed away.

problems.why: Screen-only again, but the prose and the starter disagree on naming and the sample tests are the only thing pinning the return type. The screenshot has to be read carefully, not skimmed.

screen.title: Highest and Lowest
statement: In this little assignment you are given a string of space separated numbers, and have to return the highest and lowest number.
Notes: all numbers are valid Int32, no need to validate them. There will always be at least one number in the input string. The input string will always be space separated.

expected.title: Highest and Lowest
expected.notes: The heading is the title on screen ("Highest and Lowest"), but the function is highAndLow -- the starter wins over the prose. The sample tests return a string like "42 -9", so an array or an object is wrong however plausible it looks.

problems.why: The whole problem arrives as speech while the screen shows a catalogue page. The screen decides whether there is anything to solve, so the right answer is the bail -- speech never licenses inventing an exercise.

screen.title: Kata Catalogue
screen.description: The site's problem list, sorted by rank. Nothing is opened.

spoken.text: Right, next one. Write me a function that takes a list of integers and returns the length of the longest run of consecutive equal values.
So for one, one, two, two, two, three you would get three, because the twos run three long.

expected.title: No exercise on screen
expected.notes: Exactly `# No exercise on screen` plus one sentence naming what is there instead (the kata catalogue). No code block, and no attempt at the spoken problem. This is the bail rule's sharpest edge: the transcript is a hint about what is being asked, never a source of truth about what is on screen.

problems.scriptedAnswer:
# No exercise on screen

The window is showing Codewars' kata catalogue, with no kata opened.

problems.why: The same rule with different furniture: a call window rather than a kata site, so nothing on screen even resembles an editor.

screen.title: Interview room
screen.description: A video call, 14:02 elapsed. Two participants, screen share off.

spoken.text: Okay, here's the next one. Given a string containing round, square and curly brackets, return true if they're balanced and correctly nested.
Open square, open round, close round, close square is balanced. Open round, close square is not.
Take your time, and talk me through the data structure you'd reach for.

expected.title: No exercise on screen
expected.notes: Bail again. Worth running even though the previous problem covers the same rule: a fully-stated spoken problem with worked examples is the most tempting thing to answer from the transcript alone.

problems.scriptedAnswer:
# No exercise on screen

The window is showing a video call, with no exercise or editor visible.

problems.why: The exercise is on the screen and the speech constrains how it should be solved. Both have to reach the model in one request, and the spoken constraint has to actually steer the answer.

screen.title: Reverse String
statement: Reverse a string. For example, the string "cool" becomes "looc".
Reversing strings, or manipulating them in place, is a common interview exercise.
constraints: The input is always a string.
The empty string reverses to itself.

spoken.text: Let's do the one on your screen.
Do it iteratively though — no slicing tricks, and no recursion. I want to see the loop.
And make sure the empty string still comes back empty.

expected.title: Reverse String
expected.notes: The signature, the title and the language all come from the screen. The transcript only decides which of several correct solutions to write: an explicit loop, not text[::-1] and not recursion. The answer should say in one clause that the spoken constraint steered it.

problems.scriptedAnswer:
# Reverse String

```python
def reverse(text):
    reversed_text = ""
    for character in text:
        reversed_text = character + reversed_text
    return reversed_text
```

Built iteratively rather than with a slice or recursion, as asked out loud: each character is prepended to what has been reversed so far. An empty string never enters the loop and comes back empty, which the first sample test pins.

O(n) time in Python's amortized string concatenation, O(n) space for the result.

problems.why: The screen is ambiguous where it is cut off, and the speech resolves the ambiguity. This is the case the transcript feature exists for.

screen.title: Two Sum
statement: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to target.
You can return the answer in any order.
constraints: Follow-up: can you come up with an algorithm that is less than…
screen.starterCode:
class Solution:
    def twoSum(self, nums: List[int], target: int) -> List[int]:

spoken.text: For the one you're looking at — assume there's exactly one valid answer, and you can't use the same element twice.
And I want it in linear time. Not the double loop.

expected.title: Two Sum
expected.notes: The constraints panel is cut off on screen, so the uniqueness guarantee and the linear-time requirement come from the speech. Expect a single-pass hash map keyed by complement, the class-wrapped signature reproduced exactly, and one clause saying the spoken constraint chose the approach.
